吉賈克琴琴身多以杏木製作，亦見棗木、桑木、核桃木、桃木、梨木與小葉楊；共鳴箱常為: The body of the ghijak is mostly of apricot wood, though jujube, mulberry, walnut, peach, pear and small-leaved poplar are also used; the resonator is often a wooden hemisphere or bowl covered with horse or donkey skin, and there are also metal cylinder or tin-can resonators. The bridge may be apricot or paulownia wood, the soundpost pine; early bridges were sometimes made of almond shell. Modern strings are mostly steel, replacing the traditional horsehair or gut. The foot may be iron, and the decoration includes camel bone, yak horn and black-and-white plastic; hide glue, fish glue or plastic glue is used for joining. The materials of the remaining parts are not recorded.
吉賈克琴見於阿富汗、烏茲別克、維吾爾、塔吉克、土庫曼、卡拉卡爾帕克等族群音樂。多: The ghijak is found in the music of Afghan, Uzbek, Uyghur, Tajik, Turkmen and Karakalpak peoples. The Dolan ghijak is commonly used for the Dolan muqam, folk meshrep and dastan accompaniment; the improved ghijak, besides these contexts, is one of the main accompanying instruments of the Twelve Muqam and is also used in Uyghur national orchestras. The Hami ghijak is mostly found in the Hami muqam and in folk music such as 'Shadiyane'. In the Qing court's Hui-bu music it was called 'harjak'. Ekrem Umar and Adil Abliz have performed 'The Age of Happiness' and 'Ushshaq Muqam' on the programme Feng Hua Guo Yue.
吉賈克琴（艾捷克）以弓摩擦琴弦發聲，共鳴箱與共鳴弦影響音色。多朗艾捷克音色厚實、: The ghijak (also called ajiek) sounds by the friction of bow on string, and the resonator and sympathetic strings shape the timbre. The Dolan ghijak has a thick, hoarse, rough tone and a range of about c1-c2 or d1-d2; the improved ghijak has no sympathetic strings, its tone clear and somewhat thin, and its range reaches g-g3; the Hami ghijak sounds through a metal cylinder resonator, with a clear, slightly metallic tone. The volume changes with the right-hand bowing and the size of the resonator. It is close to the Persian kamancheh, but the Hami ghijak places the bow between the main strings, while the Dolan ghijak has sympathetic strings.
吉賈克琴（艾捷克）名稱見於十世紀手稿，當時琴橋以杏仁殼製成；十五世紀波斯細密畫中: The name of the ghijak (ajiek) appears in a tenth-century manuscript, when its bridge was made of almond shell; the form shown in fifteenth-century Persian miniatures is already close to the modern one. There are many accounts of its origin; the mainstream view holds that it comes from Persia, that it is fairly close to the kamancheh, and that it spread among Afghan, Uzbek, Uyghur, Tajik, Turkmen and Karakalpak peoples and in Xinjiang. In the Qing court's Hui-bu music it was called harjak, and documents also use the name eyi ajiek. In the early 1950s, under the direction of Mai Miao, Duan Qiang designed and Semet Abdulla built the improved ajiek, which was then promoted throughout Xinjiang and became one of the main accompanying instruments of the Twelve Muqam.

The ghijak (ajiek) is a bowed string instrument of Central Asia, a chordophone of the 321.3 bowed class, close to the Persian kamancheh. Some forms have four strings, and the resonator may be bowl-shaped, hemispherical or box-shaped, some covered with skin, some made of metal; in playing the instrument rests on the left thigh, the bow is drawn across the strings and the left hand stops them. It is used by Afghans, Uzbeks, Uyghurs, Tajiks, Turkmen, Karakalpaks and in Xinjiang in China, commonly in muqam, folk meshrep and dastan accompaniment, and also in national orchestras.

演奏多朗艾捷克与改良艾捷克时，常采坐姿，挺胸抬头，将琴置于左腿上，左手持琴杆，右: When playing the Dolan and improved ajiek the player usually sits upright with the chest open, sets the instrument on the left thigh, holds the neck with the left hand and the bow in the right, and sounds it by drawing the bow across the strings; the left fingertips touch the main strings lightly, using vibrato, slides, trills and pulls, while the right hand changes the bowing. The bass improved ajiek is held much like a cello. The Hami ajiek is played kneeling, with the drum-shaped resonator on the left thigh and the first joint of the fingers touching the strings lightly. Beginners should first settle the sitting position and the placing of the instrument, then practise touching the strings and bowing.
